preamble: Voicing and spirantization turn the uvular stop [q] into the voiced uvular fricative or approximant [ʁ] between vowels. In Kazakh, morpheme-final /q/ surfaces as [ʁ] before a vowel-initial suffix and often across a word boundary. In South Bolivian Quechua, a voiced continuant [ʁ] is the most frequent intervocalic realization of /q/, even though the sound behaves as a stop in the phonology. Huaylas Quechua has a similar [ʁ] allophone. Sudanese Arabic /q/ > [ɣ] is velar, so it does not belong in this cell.

examples.note: Morpheme-final non-coronal stops are voiced and spirantized before a vowel-initial suffix. After a sonorant the stop stays voiceless, as in халқы 'nation-POSS.3' with [q].
Spirantization can also apply across a word boundary in connected speech.
Acoustic study of eight speakers: a voiced continuant, transcribed [ʁ], is the most common intervocalic realization of /q/. It is often closer to an approximant than a fricative.
Intervocalic token shown in Gallagher (2023), Figure 4.
In Pacaraos the coda reflex is voiceless (*suqta > huχta, *pusaq > puwaχ).
Proto-Lezgic fortis *q: (*qː) is continued as the voiced uvular fricative /ʁ/ (Cyrillic гъ, transliterated ġ); Tabasaran jiġ 'day' shows the same reflex
Written with гъ, the same letter that spells /ʁ/ in Lezgian
Single intervocalic q became the uvular fricative written r; West Greenlandic keeps q in aleq, aleqaq.
